summary: Reports the state of standardization of Internet protocols as decided by the Internet Activities Board, listing which protocols have which standards status. It is now historic and was replaced by RFC 1540.

plainLanguage.summary: A report card that says which Internet rules are official, which are still being tested, and which are retired.

subtitle: The authoritative registry of Internet protocol standards and their status.

tldr.problem: By 1993, the Internet had grown significantly and needed a current, authoritative list showing which protocols are official standards, which are experimental, and which have been superseded.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1500 updates the protocol standards list and refines the standardization process definitions. It categorizes protocols by maturity level (Standard, Draft Standard, Proposed Standard, Experimental, Informational, Historic) and requirement level (Required, Recommended, Elective, Limited Use, Not Recommended).
tldr.outcome: This 1993 edition of the standards list was replaced by RFC 1540 in 1995 as the standards landscape continued to evolve.

today: RFC 1540 replaced this document. RFC 1500 is Historic and documents the state of Internet protocol standards as they stood in August 1993.

sections.title: Overview of Internet Standards
sections.content:
RFC 1500 is the Internet Architecture Board official publication listing the state of Internet protocol standardization as of August 1993. It serves as the authoritative reference for determining which RFC documents define the current standards for each Internet protocol.

The document emphasizes that all Internet standards are published as RFCs, but not all RFCs are standards. The RFC series includes research documents, meeting notes, historical records, and informational papers alongside the formal standards. This memo clarifies which RFCs document standards at each maturity level.
sections.plainLanguage: The Internet was growing fast in 1993, and developers needed to know which protocols were official to use. This document listed all the protocols, organized by how official they were and whether you had to use them.

sections.title: Protocol States and Statuses
sections.content:
Every protocol has a maturity level showing its stage in standardization. Standard protocols are officially approved by the IESG and assigned STD numbers. Draft Standard protocols are under active consideration. Proposed Standard protocols are candidates for standardization. Experimental protocols document research work. Informational protocols come from vendors or other standards bodies. Historic protocols have been superseded or are no longer in use.

A protocol also has a requirement level. Required protocols must be implemented by all systems. Recommended protocols should be implemented. Elective protocols are optional. Limited Use protocols apply only in special circumstances. Not Recommended protocols should generally be avoided.
sections.plainLanguage: Each protocol gets two labels. One shows how tested it is: Standard (approved), Draft Standard (almost approved), Proposed Standard (being reviewed), Experimental (for research only), Informational (from elsewhere), or Historic (outdated). The other shows how much you must use it: Required (everyone), Recommended (you should), Elective (your choice), Limited (special cases), or Not Recommended (skip it).

sections.title: How Protocols Advance to Standard Status
sections.content:
Protocols reach standard status through a formal progression managed by the IETF. A proposed standard must wait at least 6 months before advancing to draft standard, and draft standards must wait at least 4 months before becoming standards. This delay allows the community to test and comment on the protocol.

Before advancing from proposed to draft standard, a protocol must have at least two independent implementations. Moving to standard status requires operational experience and demonstrated interoperability between at least two implementations. The IESG must recommend advancement at each step.
sections.plainLanguage: Protocols climb a ladder: Proposed Standard is the first step, Draft Standard is the next, and Standard is the top. At each step you must wait months and prove the protocol works in real life. The IETF must agree before you can move up.

sections.title: Networks and Host Requirements
sections.content:
Beyond protocol standards, the standards system references other key documents. The Host Requirements RFCs (1122 and 1123) detail requirements for Internet hosts. The Gateway Requirements (RFC 1009) covers gateway systems. These documents clarify ambiguities in the protocol specifications and provide implementation guidance.

Since different systems have different roles, not all protocols are required for all systems. A router has different requirements than a desktop computer. The requirement levels allow for flexibility while maintaining interoperability.
sections.plainLanguage: Not every computer on the Internet does the same job. A router needs different protocols than a laptop. The standards list says which protocols are required for different kinds of systems, so everything can talk to everything else.

sections.title: Status in 1993
sections.content:
RFC 1500 captured the state of Internet protocol standards in August 1993, when the Internet was entering a period of rapid growth and commercialization. The document listed the major protocols then in use: IP, TCP, UDP for transport; Telnet and FTP for applications; SMTP for mail; DNS for naming; SNMP for management.

RFC 1540 replaced this edition with an updated list as the standards landscape continued to evolve. RFC 1500 is now Historic.
sections.plainLanguage: In 1993, the Internet had about 30 protocols that were official standards. This list showed which ones you had to use, which were recommended, and which were experimental. Now that version is outdated, but it shows what the Internet looked like back then.
